Proportional blame ignores intention, which is half of what makes an act what it is, but a good intention does not end the builders' duty to find and stop the harm. An act is weighed by the volition behind it as much as by what follows. Builders who intended to help, and took real care, acted from a sound intention, and blaming them as if they had acted carelessly ignores half of what their act was.

Good intention cannot be a blanket excuse. A well-meaning builder who stops checking once the system ships is not acting from care any longer, and the damage that follows is theirs in a way the first unforeseen harm was not. A team's careful chatbot gives harmful advice to a user in crisis. They are not culpable for an unforeseeable failure, but they publish what happened and retrain it within the week.

A Utilitarian will object that intention is invisible and irrelevant to the people harmed, so blame should track what deters future harm, not the builders' inner states. Intention is not invisible in practice: it shows in how carefully builders tested and how fast they respond. And a rule that blames the careful as much as the careless removes the reason to be careful at all. The builders are still called to attend to the injured, but attending is not the same as being to blame.

A Buddhist Ethicist rejects the motion, with a warning: care and good intention lessen blame, yet they never excuse a builder from looking hard at what their system goes on doing. What happened arose from many conditions: the data, the users, the setting, the builders' choices. Blame in proportion to harm treats the builders as the single cause, when compassion asks for an honest account of all the conditions and of their part among them.

Good intention cannot be a blanket excuse. A well-meaning builder who stops checking once the system ships is not acting from care any longer, and the damage that follows is theirs in a way the first unforeseen harm was not. A well-meaning startup's tool harms users and the founders point to their good intentions. Their intention was sound at launch; their refusal to look again is not.

The builders are still called to attend to the injured, but attending is not the same as being to blame.

Volition weighs as much as what follows, so builders who acted with care and good intention are not to blame in proportion to the harm, though they stay bound to keep examining the system. The discourse to Rahula asks that an act be examined after it is done, and if it is found to harm oneself or another, that it be acknowledged and not repeated. That is the builders' duty here: to admit the harm and change what caused it.
